Part 01 · The thesis

The wall is the business.

South Africa does not have a wall shortage. It has a wall performance problem. Masonry is slow, heavy and thermally poor. Alternative systems are fragmented, under-certified and sold as science projects. The country approves about R44 billion of private residential building plans a year; the wall is where the money, the time and the risk sit.

Five systems can change that. They are not five versions of the same business. One is an import-and-certify play. One is a distribution-and-install play for a product that already has local approval. One is a prefabricated envelope for a niche. One is a concrete system for premium structures. One is a factory.

The models share a market and a method. They do not share a risk profile. AAC can sell into a bonded build next month; SYSTEM 3E cannot sell into one until a certificate is in hand. Perlite has the best gross margin and the worst cash cycle. SIPs have the fastest envelope and the weakest lender story. ICF sits in the middle: a familiar trade, a premium customer, a concrete supply chain that can break a schedule.

That is why this report is five models, not one plan with four comparison rows. A comparison tells you which product is cheapest. A model tells you what you have to build, hire, certify, sell and survive before the product earns a rand.

The numbers

2026 estimates, not quotes

All prices are ex VAT, in rand, at the installed or factory gate stated. Where a supplier does not publish a price, the number is modelled and marked. Replace it with a written quote before capital is released.

The stages

Prove, scale, localise

Stage 1 proves demand. Stage 2 scales the channel. Stage 3 localises or expands. Capital is released in gates, not in one cheque. Each model has a walk-away test.

The ranking

An order of operations

The score is a weighted reading of capital efficiency, gross margin, speed to revenue, regulatory ease, competitive position, scalability and supply resilience. It is not a beauty contest.

What this report is not. It is not a supplier brochure, a valuation or a building contract. It is a set of models to be tested. The first test is always a written quote; the second is a paid project; the third is a certificate or an engineer’s signature.

Gross margin by model

Modelled, ex VAT, at the stated price
The cheapest wall is not the best business. AAC sells at R1,350/m² and earns R470/m². SYSTEM 3E sells at R3,350/m² and earns R939/m². The cheaper product has the lower margin per square metre but the faster cash cycle and the lower capital. In a market where the customer is credit-constrained, speed and financeability beat a premium price.

The gross margin is per square metre of wall, before opex. It is not a net margin and it is not a return on capital. The ranking at the end weights capital and regulation as well as margin.

Model 01 of 05 · Wall systems · South Africa 2026

SYSTEM 3E

Import → certify → localise

The highest-margin wall in the study, and the longest road to revenue. A Polish dry-stack expanded-perlite system that needs no mortar, glue or water. The business is importing it, getting it accepted, and then making it here.

3.45/5 Back behind a certificate

Prepared for Ricardo Maio · 2 November 2026 · Batman / Infinity Brands

SYSTEM 3E is a wall made almost entirely of expanded perlite. The blocks click together dry. No mortar bed, no glue, no water on site. A small crew can close a shell in days, not weeks. The manufacturer claims about 100 m² of wall in 24 hours; treat that as a factory claim until a South African crew repeats it.

The commercial gap is certification and supply, not demand. No South African project is listed. A builder cannot get a bond on a system the banks and insurers have not seen. The first business is therefore not a factory. It is a certification and demonstration business with a product attached.

01

Market

The market is the same R44.4bn residential build that every model in this report addresses. SYSTEM 3E’s addressable slice is narrower: premium eco homes, backyard cottages, farm buildings and small commercial work where a cash buyer can accept an uncertified system.

Market sizing for SYSTEM 3E, 2026.

TAMR44.4bnAnnualised private residential building plans, Stats SA P5041.1 (July 2026).
Wall systems · 20%R8.88bnWall share of build value; the rest is services, finishes, fees and land.
SAMR1.981bn1,250 premium homes × 150 m² × R2,800; 8,000 cottages × 40 m² × R2,800; 2,000 small commercial × 100 m² × R2,800.

The SAM is deliberately conservative on price: it uses R2,800/m², below the R3,350/m² installed price, because the first customers are price-sensitive cash builders. The capture is 1.2% of SAM, not a national fantasy.

02

Product

  • About 99% expanded perlite. Volcanic glass is popped like popcorn, then bound into a block. The wall is light, self-insulating and fire-resistant.
  • Dry-stack click assembly. No mortar, glue or water. The blocks have a click profile; a small crew can close a shell without a wet trade.
  • Load-bearing for single-storey and low-rise homes, subject to engineering. It is a wall system, not a frame; the load path still has to be designed.
  • No listed South African project. The product works in physics; the certificate is what makes it work in a bank.

Primary sources: SYSTEM 3E product page · B2B page.

What has to be true. The product must pass a South African test, not a brochure. For SYSTEM 3E, the first proof is a certificate and eight paid projects. Everything else is arithmetic.

10

Verdict

Back behind a certificate

The product is good; the certificate is the business. SYSTEM 3E has the highest gross margin in the study, but it also has the longest cash cycle and the thinnest supply chain. Do not spend the plant capital until the certificate is in hand and eight projects have been paid for. If the certificate slips, the business is a demo company, not a manufacturer.

Best forA founder with patience, a certification budget and a cash-build customer base.
Not forA team that needs revenue in 90 days.

AAC

Supply & install

The unglamorous winner. AAC is already manufactured in South Africa, already specified under SANS, and already accepted by engineers. The business is not inventing a product; it is building a reliable supply-and-install channel for a product that works.

4.00/5 Back first

AAC is concrete with air in it. Autoclaved aerated concrete is made from cement, lime, sand, gypsum, water and aluminium powder; the aluminium reacts to form bubbles, and the mix is cured in an autoclave. The result is a block about one-third the weight of dense concrete, with good thermal performance and a four-hour fire rating.

Aertec manufactures in Cape Town and Durban. The blocks are 600 × 250 mm, 100/150/200 mm thick, 6.67 units per m². The product standard is SANS 50771-4. This is the lowest-regulatory-risk wall in the study. The gap is installation quality and builder education, not product approval.

01

Market

AAC can address general masonry, not just premium homes. The first channel is builders and developers who already specify AAC but cannot get a reliable install crew. That is a channel problem, not a product problem, and it is the cheapest problem in this report.

Market sizing for AAC, 2026.

SOM · Stage 1R4.05m3,000 m² at R1,350/m²; 0.15% of the addressable market.

The capture is deliberately small because the constraint is crew capacity, not demand. Twenty projects in Stage 1 is two crews working a full year, not a national sales campaign.

02

Product

  • 600 × 250 mm, 6.67 units/m². Available in 100, 150 and 200 mm thickness. Thin-bed mortar, not a conventional 10 mm bed.
  • Three times faster than conventional masonry. Aertec’s own case study reports a 48% time reduction and a 21% project cost saving on a six-storey Cape Town building.
  • Four-hour fire rating and 30% energy saving. The block is the insulation; no cavity fill or drywall.
  • Already in the market. Aertec lists residential, commercial, student accommodation, hospitality and industrial projects from 2019 to 2024.

Primary sources: Aertec technical data · Aertec projects · Gissa / Everite AAC.

What has to be true. The product must pass a South African test, not a brochure. For AAC, the first proof is a supply agreement and twenty paid projects. Everything else is arithmetic.

Model 03 of 05 · Wall systems · South Africa 2026

SIPs

Prefabricate the envelope

The fastest envelope, and the hardest sell to a bank. SIPs are a structural sandwich: two skins and an insulating core. The business is prefabricated envelopes for eco homes, cottages and additions — not mass housing.

2.80/5 Hold

2026 estimates, ex VAT, in rand — not quotes

A structural insulated panel is a sandwich. OSB or cement board skins are bonded to an EPS, PUR or PIR core. The panel carries load, insulates, and arrives cut to size. A crew can close a house in days. The product is proven in cold climates and high-wind markets; in South Africa it is a niche.

The local supply chain is thin. Isowall makes insulated panels, but the structural SIP market is not a mature local category. Most suppliers are small, project-based, or import. That is the opportunity and the risk: you would be creating a category, not taking share.

01

Market

SIPs are not a mass-masonry substitute. The first market is the self-build eco home, the guest farm and the addition where speed and insulation matter more than a bond. That is a real market, but it is a small one.

Market sizing for SIPs, 2026.
LayerValueBasis
TAMR44.4bnAnnualised private residential building plans, Stats SA P5041.1 (July 2026).
SIP-addressable · 10%R888mEco homes, cottages, additions and light commercial envelopes.
SAMR424m2,000 projects × 80 m² × R2,650/m².
SOM · Stage 1R2.86m1,080 m² at R2,650/m²; 0.7% of SAM.

The SAM assumes 2,000 projects a year. That is not a published statistic; it is a modelled segment built from the number of small builders and architects active in the eco-home niche. Treat it as a planning assumption, not a census.

02

Product

  • Two skins, one core. OSB or cement board bonded to EPS, PUR or PIR. The panel is the structure and the insulation in one component.
  • Fast envelope. Panels arrive cut to size; a crew can close a house in days, with less site waste and fewer trades.
  • Thin walls, high insulation. A 150 mm SIP wall delivers a better U-value than a 230 mm brick wall, with a thinner footprint.
  • Fire, moisture, termite and lender acceptance are the gates. A SIP house can be technically excellent and still fail a bond.

Primary sources: Isowall SIP guide · Premier SIP cost guide · SIP panel price benchmark.

What has to be true. The product must pass a South African test, not a brochure. For SIPs, the first proof is an insurer and a paid project. Everything else is arithmetic.

ICF

Concrete inside foam

Concrete strength, foam insulation, and a familiar trade. ICF is the easiest premium upgrade to sell to an engineer and the easiest to get wrong on site.

3.60/5 Back second

Prepared for Ricardo Maio · 2 November 2026 · Batman / Infinity Brands
2026 estimates, ex VAT, in rand — not quotes

An insulated concrete form is a hollow foam block. You stack it, place rebar, and fill it with concrete. The foam stays in place as insulation; the concrete becomes the structure. The result is a strong, quiet, thermally stable wall with no formwork to strip.

South Africa already has a supply chain. Isowall has manufactured EPS since 1993 and sells ICF blocks; ICF Building SA distributes a local system. The blocks are 1,200 × 300 mm, 120/150/180 mm thick. The concrete is typically 15 MPa with Y8 rebar. This is not a new category. It is a category with weak installation capacity.

01

Market

ICF is over-specified for a standard R1.2m house. The first market is the premium home, the pool, the safe room and the small commercial building where strength, quiet and thermal stability are worth a premium.

The premium-home count is a modelled segment, not a published census. It is built from the top 10% of private residential plans by value. The first channel is architects and developers who already build at that level.

02

Product

  • EPS hollow block, concrete core. Stack the block, place rebar, pour concrete. The foam stays as insulation; the concrete is the structure.
  • 1,200 × 300 mm, 120/150/180 mm. Typically 15 MPa concrete with Y8 rebar; three rows per pour.
  • Strong, quiet, thermally stable. Good for premium homes, pools, safe rooms and commercial buildings.
  • No formwork to strip. The form is the finished insulation. That is the speed advantage over conventional concrete.

Primary sources: ICF Building SA cost guide · Isowall ICF build guide · ICF market data.

Perlite block

Make the block here

The only model that makes the product itself. A local plant turning expanded perlite, cement and sand into a lightweight insulating block. Highest margin at scale, highest capital, longest ramp.

3.05/5 Back later

Prepared for Ricardo Maio · 2 November 2026 · Batman / Infinity Brands

Perlite is a volcanic glass that expands up to 20 times its volume when heated. Mixed with cement, it makes a block that is light, insulating and fire-resistant. It is not a dry-stack system like SYSTEM 3E; it is a conventional masonry block with a better aggregate.

South Africa has the raw material. Pratley Minerals sells expanded perlite from Gauteng and Cape Town; a 100-litre bag retails around R123 ex depot. The block can be made on a standard vibro-compaction line. The business is a plant, a mix design, a certification file and a distribution channel. It is the most capital-intensive of the five, and the most defensible if it works.

01

Market

The first market is builders’ merchants and builders who want a lightweight block that lays like masonry and insulates better than concrete. That is a broad, unglamorous market; it is also the only one in this report that can absorb a 75,000 m²/year plant.

Market sizing for Perlite block, 2026.
LayerValueBasis
TAMR44.4bnAnnualised private residential building plans, Stats SA P5041.1 (July 2026).
Insulating masonry · 25%R2.22bnWalls where thermal performance is worth a premium.
SAMR912.5m5,000 premium homes × 150 m² × R950 = R712.5m; commercial and agricultural R200m.
SOM · Stage 1R8.55m9,000 m² at R950/m²; 0.9% of SAM and 12% of plant capacity.

The plant is sized at 75,000 m²/year, not at the SAM. That is deliberate: the business needs a product that can sell beyond the premium niche. Stage 1 runs at 12% utilisation, which is the real test of the sales channel.

02

Product

  • Expanded perlite, cement and sand. A lightweight insulating block, not a dry-stack system. It lays with standard mortar and standard tools.
  • Density 800–1,000 kg/m³; 3.5–5 MPa; thermal conductivity 0.12–0.18 W/mK. Non-combustible; good for walls that need insulation without a cavity.
  • Local raw material. Pratley supplies expanded perlite from Gauteng and Cape Town; the block machine can be imported or bought locally.
  • The mix is the product. A block that passes a trial mix but fails SANS 1215 is not a product. Test before you pour the slab.

Primary sources: Pratley construction perlite · SANS 1215 explained · CISH block-machine prices.

What has to be true. The product must pass a South African test, not a brochure. For Perlite block, the first proof is a SANS 1215 mix and 5,000 m² of orders. Everything else is arithmetic.

Part 08 · The ranking

The order is the answer.

Five good models, one balance sheet. The ranking is not a verdict on the products; it is a verdict on the sequence. AAC first, ICF second, SYSTEM 3E behind a certificate, perlite when the channel is proven, SIPs as a specialist arm.

Weighted scorecard. Capital 20%, gross margin 20%, speed 15%, regulation 15%, competition 15%, scalability 10%, supply 5%.
RankModelCapitalMarginSpeedRegulationCompetitionScaleSupplyWeighted
1AAC53552444.00
2ICF44433343.60
3SYSTEM 3E35324423.45
4Perlite block14234543.05
5SIPs33323322.80

Scores are 1–5, where 5 is best. Capital: 5 means low capital intensity. Regulation: 5 means easy approval. Competition: 5 means a weak competitive field. Supply: 5 means a resilient supply chain.

The ranking is an order of operations, not a beauty contest. AAC wins because it can earn next quarter. SYSTEM 3E has the best margin and the worst timing. A portfolio that starts with SYSTEM 3E runs out of cash before it runs out of market.
01

The order

  1. 01
    AAC — Start here.

    It funds the rest. Lowest regulatory risk, lowest capital, fastest revenue, and a product that already has local approval. The first 20 projects teach you the customer, the crew and the cash cycle.

  2. 02
    ICF — Add it next.

    Same customer list, different trade. Premium homes, pools, safe rooms and small commercial. The margin is better than AAC and the certification path is shorter than SIPs. Concrete supply is the constraint.

  3. 03
    SYSTEM 3E — Certify with the cash flow.

    Do not build the plant. Use AAC and ICF cash to fund the Agrément file, one container and two demo units. The plant only after the certificate and eight paid projects.

  4. 04
    Perlite block — Build the plant later.

    The best gross margin and the best localisation story, but R7.8m before a rand and 12% utilisation to break even. It is a second-stage asset, not a first venture.

  5. 05
    SIPs — Quote it, do not build around it.

    A useful specialist arm for the client who asks for it. The lender is the real customer, the fire test is expensive and the local panel supply is thin.

02

Capital versus margin

Where each model sits

Boundaries: R3.0m funding · 25% gross margin

The boundaries are the study’s midpoints, not universal laws. The point is the shape: AAC and ICF are cheap enough to build first; SYSTEM 3E and perlite need capital and patience; SIPs sit below the margin line.

The one-line answer

If Ricardo wants one business: AAC supply and install. If he wants the best long-term asset: the perlite block plant, after the channel is proven. If he wants the highest margin and can wait: SYSTEM 3E behind a certificate. If he wants a specialist arm: SIPs, quoted when asked.

Part 09 · Capital

What each cheque buys.

The five models are not a menu to buy all at once. They are a sequence of cheques. At R7.7m there is a fork: the channel portfolio, or the perlite plant. Not both.

Capital ladder. Figures are total funding, including working capital.
ChequeWhat it buysWhat it returns in Stage 1
R2.5mAAC onlyR1.6m capex + R0.9m working capital. 20 projects, R4.05m revenue, R1.41m gross profit, R0.26m EBITDA.
R5.2mAAC + ICFTwo install crews, one warehouse, shared back office. Combined Stage 1 revenue R7.57m, gross profit R2.61m, EBITDA R0.41m.
R7.7mAAC + ICF + SYSTEM 3E certificationR2.5m seed for SYSTEM 3E; no plant. Certification, one container, two demo units. The plant waits for the certificate.
R7.8mPerlite plant insteadA standalone choice, not a bolt-on. R4.0m equity + R3.76m equipment finance. Only with 20,000 m²/year of committed demand.
The R7.7m fork. The channel portfolio buys three businesses and a certification file. The perlite plant buys one factory. The portfolio has more ways to win and more ways to learn; the plant has a higher gross margin and a longer payback. If the objective is a durable operating company, take the portfolio first.
Do

Fund the channel first

AAC and ICF share a customer, a warehouse and a back office. The second business is cheaper than the first because the overhead is already paid.

Do not

Fund two plants

SYSTEM 3E and perlite both want a factory. A portfolio with two plants and no channel is a capital allocation error dressed as diversification.

The Stage 1 EBITDA figures are pre-tax, pre-interest and pre-depreciation. They do not include the founder’s salary unless stated in opex. The capital ladder is a planning tool, not a valuation.

Part 10 · China

China can sell you the machine. It cannot sell you the certificate.

Three of the five can be sourced from China. Two cannot be copied cheaply. The distinction is not patriotism; it is freight, patents and the cost of proof.

What China can supply, model by model.
ModelChina optionVerdict
SYSTEM 3ENo. Polish product, patented in China, Europe and the USA. Heavy: about 213 m² per 40ft container.Import from Poland; localise under licence at Stage 3.
AACA Chinese AAC plant is available, but South Africa already has Aertec in Cape Town and Durban.Buy the block locally; do not build a plant to compete with an incumbent.
SIPsYes, panels and presses are available. The constraint is fire testing and lender acceptance, not supply.Import panels or a small line only after a lender says yes.
ICFYes, moulds and block machines are available. The local ICF supply chain already exists.Buy local blocks; import a mould only for a proprietary shape.
PerliteYes, block machines and expanded perlite lines are available. CISH quotes USD 120k–450k for a semi-automatic plant.Import the machine, make the block locally, test the mix.

SYSTEM 3E is not a Chinese product. It is Polish. The blocks are patented in China, Europe and the USA, and the economics are dominated by freight: about 213 m² of wall per 40ft container. A Chinese copy would still have to solve the same weight problem, and it would still need a South African certificate.

AAC is the opposite case. The product is already made here. Aertec has plants in Cape Town and Durban and a project list from 2019 to 2024. A Chinese plant would compete with an incumbent that already has approvals, customers and a cost base in rand. The opportunity is the channel, not the factory.

Perlite is the one model where a Chinese machine makes sense. CISH quotes a semi-automatic block plant at USD 120,000–450,000. The machine is a commodity; the mix design and the SANS 1215 test are not. Import the steel, make the block, prove the mix.

The import trap. A cheap machine is not a cheap business. Duty, freight, installation, commissioning, spares and the learning curve arrive after the invoice. Model the landed cost, not the FOB price.
Part 11 · Method

How the numbers were built.

Every model uses the same method so the comparison is fair. The inputs differ; the arithmetic does not. Where a number is modelled, it is marked. Where a supplier publishes a price, the link is in the sources.

Market

TAM, SAM, SOM

TAM is the annualised value of private residential building plans passed, from Stats SA P5041.1 (July 2026). The wall-system slice is 20% of TAM. SAM is a segment count × average size × model price; SOM is Stage 1 volume × model price. The segment counts are planning assumptions, not census data.

Financials

Pre-tax, pre-interest

Revenue is m² × price. Direct cost is m² × cost. Gross profit is revenue minus direct cost. EBITDA is gross profit minus opex, before depreciation, interest and tax. Capex excludes working capital.

Pricing

Ex VAT, 2026

All prices are ex VAT. Where a supplier quotes a range, the model uses the midpoint or the conservative end. The price-floor table tests the same cost base at four prices.

FX

30 October 2026

1 USD = R16.69. 1 EUR = R18.65. 1 PLN = R4.234. The SYSTEM 3E landed cost uses PLN and USD; the perlite plant uses USD. A 10% FX move changes the import models more than the local ones.

What is quoted, what is modelled, and what must be tested first.
ModelQuoted inputModelled inputFirst test
SYSTEM 3ENone publicBlock price, freight, duty, labourWritten landed-cost quote
AACBlock range; project referencesInstalled labour, opexSupply agreement and BQ quote
SIPsPanel benchmarks (US, EU)Local panel price, labour, certificationPanel quote and lender position
ICFBlock range; concrete benchmarkRebar, labour, pumpEngineer and pump quote
PerliteMachine range; perlite bag priceMix, civils, opexTrial mix and SANS 1215 test

The models are deliberately conservative on price and capital. If a model works only with an aggressive price and a perfect build, it does not work.
